summary.text: For \(0\le q<10^L\), decimal complementation \(q\mapsto10^L-1-q\) gives both \(s(q)+s(10^L-1-q)=9L\) and \(s(5q)+s(5(10^L-1-q))=9L\), the latter by a digitwise induction tracking complementary multiplication-by-5 carries. Hence the signed increments at complementary indices are negatives, and pairing them while moving outward from \(m=10^L/2-1\) yields equality of the corresponding cumulative sums.

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
s(n)=\text{the sum of the decimal digits of }n,
\]
and define
\[
D(n)=s(5n)-s(n),\qquad t(n)=\operatorname{sign}(D(n)).
\]
Thus the sequence in question is the cumulative sum
\[
a(n)=\sum_{r=0}^{n}t(r).
\]
We will prove the stronger pointwise antisymmetry
\[
t(q)+t(10^L-1-q)=0\qquad(0\le q<10^L),                 \tag{1}
\]
and then deduce the desired symmetry of the cumulative sums.

We first establish the required decimal digit-sum identities.

For any nonnegative integers \(A,d\) with \(0\le d<10\), appending the digit \(d\) to the decimal expansion of \(A\) gives
\[
s(10A+d)=s(A)+d.                                      \tag{2}
\]
This also holds when \(A=d=0\), since both sides are zero.

### Ordinary decimal complements

For every \(L\ge0\) and every \(q<10^L\),
\[
s(q)+s(10^L-1-q)=9L.                                 \tag{3}
\]
Indeed, this is the usual identity for an \(L\)-digit number, allowing leading zeroes: the digits of \(10^L-1-q\) are obtained by replacing every digit \(d\) of \(q\) by \(9-d\).

For completeness, it can also be proved inductively from (2). For \(L=0\), the condition \(q<1\) forces \(q=0\), and the result is immediate. For the induction step, write
\[
q=10A+d,\qquad 0\le d<10.
\]
Since \(q<10^{L+1}\), we have \(A<10^L\), and
\[
10^{L+1}-1-q=10(10^L-1-A)+(9-d).
\]
Applying (2) to these two numbers, and then applying the induction hypothesis to \(A\), gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
s(q)+s(10^{L+1}-1-q)
 &=s(A)+d+s(10^L-1-A)+(9-d)\\
 &=9L+9=9(L+1).
\end{aligned}
\]

### Decimal complements after multiplication by \(5\)

The less immediate identity is
\[
s(5q)+s\bigl(5(10^L-1-q)\bigr)=9L                 \tag{4}
\]
for every \(q<10^L\). We prove it through a slightly more general carry identity:
\[
s(5q+c)+s\bigl(5(10^L-1-q)+(4-c)\bigr)=9L+4       \tag{5}
\]
whenever \(q<10^L\) and \(0\le c\le4\).

We prove (5) by induction on \(L\). If \(L=0\), then \(q=0\), so the left side is
\[
s(c)+s(4-c)=c+(4-c)=4,
\]
as required.

Now suppose (5) is known for length \(L\), and let \(q<10^{L+1}\). Write
\[
q=10A+d,
\]
where \(0\le d<10\) and \(A<10^L\). Define the carry and final digit produced by multiplying the last digit by \(5\) and adding \(c\):
\[
C=\left\lfloor\frac{5d+c}{10}\right\rfloor,
\qquad
R=(5d+c)\bmod 10.
\]
Because \(5d+c\le 5\cdot9+4=49\), we have \(0\le C\le4\). Moreover,
\[
5q+c=10(5A+C)+R.                                     \tag{6}
\]

Set
\[
Q=10^L-1-A,
\qquad B=49-(5d+c).
\]
If \(5d+c=10C+R\), then
\[
B=49-10C-R=10(4-C)+(9-R).                            \tag{7}
\]
Here \(0\le R\le9\), so (7) shows both that
\[
\left\lfloor\frac B{10}\right\rfloor=4-C
\quad\text{and}\quad
B\bmod10=9-R.                                        \tag{8}
\]
In particular, the two final digits \(R\) and \(B\bmod10\) have sum \(9\).

The decimal complement of \(q=10A+d\) is
\[
10^{L+1}-1-q=10Q+(9-d).
\]
Consequently,
\[
\begin{aligned}
5(10^{L+1}-1-q)+(4-c)
 &=5(10Q+9-d)+(4-c)\\
 &=50Q+49-(5d+c)\\
 &=10\bigl(5Q+(4-C)\bigr)+(B\bmod10),                \tag{9}
\end{aligned}
\]
where the last equality follows from (8).

Equations (6), (9), and the digit-appending identity (2) now give
\[
\begin{aligned}
&s(5q+c)+s\bigl(5(10^{L+1}-1-q)+(4-c)\bigr)\\
&\quad=s(5A+C)+R+s\bigl(5Q+(4-C)\bigr)+(B\bmod10).
\end{aligned}
\]
The induction hypothesis applies to \(A<10^L\) with carry \(C\le4\), and says
\[
s(5A+C)+s\bigl(5(10^L-1-A)+(4-C)\bigr)=9L+4.
\]
Since \(Q=10^L-1-A\), and since \(R+(B\bmod10)=9\), the preceding displayed sum is
\[
(9L+4)+9=9(L+1)+4.
\]
This completes the induction and proves (5).

We next note that, for every \(n\ge0\),
\[
s(5n+4)=s(5n)+4.                                    \tag{10}
\]
To see this, write \(n=10A+d\), with \(0\le d<10\), and let
\[
C=\left\lfloor\frac{5d}{10}\right\rfloor,
\qquad R=(5d)\bmod10.
\]
Then
\[
5n=10(5A+C)+R.
\]
The residue \(R\) is either \(0\) or \(5\), because \(5d\) modulo \(10\) is \(0\) for even \(d\) and \(5\) for odd \(d\). Hence \(R+4<10\), so adding \(4\) changes only the final decimal digit and creates no carry. By (2),
\[
s(5n+4)=s(5A+C)+(R+4)=s(5A+C)+R+4=s(5n)+4.
\]

Apply the generalized identity (5) with \(c=0\). It gives, for \(q<10^L\),
\[
s(5q)+s\bigl(5(10^L-1-q)+4\bigr)=9L+4.
\]
Using (10) with \(n=10^L-1-q\), the second digit sum is
\[
s\bigl(5(10^L-1-q)\bigr)+4.
\]
Cancelling \(4\) proves (4):
\[
s(5q)+s\bigl(5(10^L-1-q)\bigr)=9L.
\]

### Antisymmetry of the individual terms

Fix \(q<10^L\), and put
\[
y=10^L-1-q.
\]
Identity (3) says
\[
s(q)+s(y)=9L,
\]
while identity (4) says
\[
s(5q)+s(5y)=9L.
\]
Subtracting the first equality from the second gives
\[
\bigl(s(5q)-s(q)\bigr)+\bigl(s(5y)-s(y)\bigr)=0.
\]
Thus
\[
D(y)=-D(q).
\]
Since \(\operatorname{sign}(-z)=-\operatorname{sign}(z)\), including when \(z=0\), it follows that
\[
t(y)=-t(q).
\]
This is precisely (1):
\[
t(q)+t(10^L-1-q)=0.
\]

### From term antisymmetry to symmetry of cumulative sums

Let
\[
P(n)=\sum_{r=0}^{n}t(r).
\]
Suppose \(m\) satisfies
\[
2m+1=10^L-1.                                         \tag{11}
\]
We claim that
\[
P(m-i)=P(m+i)\qquad(0\le i\le m).                   \tag{12}
\]

We prove this by induction on \(i\). For \(i=0\), both sides are \(P(m)\). Now suppose the equality holds at \(i\), and suppose \(i+1\le m\). Put
\[
x=m-i.
\]
Then \(x>0\), and by (11),
\[
10^L-1-x
 =10^L-1-(m-i)
 =(2m+1)-(m-i)
 =m+i+1.                                             \tag{13}
\]
Also \(x<10^L\), so the term antisymmetry (1), together with (13), yields
\[
t(m+i+1)=-t(m-i).                                    \tag{14}
\]
The defining recurrence for cumulative sums is
\[
P(n)=P(n-1)+t(n)\quad(n>0).
\]
Therefore
\[
P(m-i)=P(m-i-1)+t(m-i),                              \tag{15}
\]
and
\[
P(m+i+1)=P(m+i)+t(m+i+1).                            \tag{16}
\]
By the induction hypothesis, \(P(m-i)=P(m+i)\); by (14), the newly added term on the right is the negative of the term removed on the left. More explicitly, (15) gives
\[
P(m-i-1)=P(m-i)-t(m-i),
\]
whereas (16), (14), and the induction hypothesis give
\[
P(m+i+1)=P(m+i)-t(m-i)=P(m-i)-t(m-i).
\]
Hence
\[
P(m-(i+1))=P(m+(i+1)).
\]
This proves (12) for all \(0\le i\le m\).

Finally, let \(k>0\), and set
\[
m_k=\frac{10^k}{2}-1.
\]
Because \(k>0\), write \(k=K+1\). Then
\[
10^k=10^{K+1}=10\cdot10^K=2(5\cdot10^K),
\]
so
\[
\frac{10^k}{2}=5\cdot10^K
\quad\text{and}\quad
m_k=5\cdot10^K-1.
\]
It follows that
\[
2m_k+1=2(5\cdot10^K-1)+1=10^k-1.
\]
Thus condition (11) holds with \(L=k\) and \(m=m_k\). Applying (12), we obtain for every \(i\) with \(0\le i\le m_k\),
\[
a(m_k-i)=P(m_k-i)=P(m_k+i)=a(m_k+i).
\]
Therefore, for every integer \(k>0\), with \(m_k=10^k/2-1\), the sequence satisfies
\[
\boxed{a(m_k-i)=a(m_k+i)\quad\text{for all }0\le i\le m_k.}
\]
